On additive bases of finite abelian groups

Weidong Gao Address: Center for Applied Mathematics, Tianjin University, Center for Applied Mathematics and KL-AAGDM, Tianjin University, Tianjin 300072, P.R. China Email address: wdgao@nankai.edu.cn and Hanbin Zhang Address: School of Mathematics (Zhuhai), Sun Yat-sen University, Zhuhai 519082, Guangdong, P.R. China Email address: zhanghb68@mail.sysu.edu.cn
Abstract.

Let GG be a finite abelian group, let pp be the smallest prime divisor of |G||G|, and let c0​(G)c_{0}(G) be the least integer tt such that every regular sequence over GG of length at least tt is an additive basis. Additive bases have been extensively studied in additive combinatorics, and the exact value of c0​(G)c_{0}(G) has been determined for many groups of rank at least three and some groups of rank two (in which case groups of the form Cp⊕Cp​nC_{p}\oplus C_{pn} turn out to be exceptional). In this paper, we continue the study of c0​(G)c_{0}(G) and obtain the following results.

  1. (1)

    Together with known results, we prove that c0​(G)=|G|/p+p−2c_{0}(G)=|G|/p+p-2 for all abelian groups GG with rank⁡(G)≥3\rank(G)\geq 3.

  2. (2)

    For distinct odd primes p<qp<q, we determine

    c0​(Cp⊕Cp​q)=p​q+2​p−3,c0​(Cq⊕Cp​q)=q2+p−2.c_{0}(C_{p}\oplus C_{pq})=pq+2p-3,\qquad c_{0}(C_{q}\oplus C_{pq})=q^{2}+p-2.
  3. (3)

    Let pp be an odd prime, let 2≤a≤b2\leq a\leq b, and let nn be a positive integer with no prime divisor smaller than pp. Then

    c0​(Cpa⊕Cpb​n)=pa+b−1​n+p−2.c_{0}(C_{p^{a}}\oplus C_{p^{b}n})=p^{a+b-1}n+p-2.
  4. (4)

    For every odd integer n≥3n\geq 3, we prove

    c0​(C3⊕C3​n)=3​n+3.c_{0}(C_{3}\oplus C_{3n})=3n+3.

Therefore, c0​(G)c_{0}(G) is determined except possibly for groups of the form Cp⊕Cp​nC_{p}\oplus C_{pn} with p≥5p\geq 5.

Key words and phrases: 
Additive basis, regular sequence, finite abelian group, Kneser’s theorem
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 11B75; Secondary 11P70, 20K01

1. Introduction

Let GG be a nontrivial finite abelian group, written additively. Let S=g1⋅…⋅gkS=g_{1}\cdot\ldots\cdot g_{k} be a sequence over GG (unordered, repetition is allowed, and gi∈Gg_{i}\in G for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k) and let σ⁡(S)=∑i=1kgi\sigma(S)=\sum^{k}_{i=1}g_{i}. We denote by T|ST\mid S for a subsequence TT of SS. We use

Σ(S)={σ(T):1≠T∣S},Σ0(S)=Σ(S)∪{0},\Sigma(S)=\{\sigma(T):1\neq T\mid S\},\qquad\Sigma_{0}(S)=\Sigma(S)\cup\{0\},

where 11 denotes the empty sequence. The sequence SS is an additive basis of GG if Σ⁡(S)=G\Sigma(S)=G. The critical number c⁡(G)c(G) is defined as the smallest integer tt such that every subset of G∖{0}G\setminus\{0\} of cardinality at least tt is an additive basis of GG. In 1964, Erdős and Heilbronn proposed the problem of determining c⁡(G)c(G), and it was completely determined by 2009 through many authors’ efforts; see [2] and the references therein, and we also refer to [11] for an important related progress. The additive basis problem has also recently been considered for finite, not necessarily abelian, groups by Qu and Gao [18].

For a subgroup H≤GH\leq G, let SHS_{H} be the subsequence consisting of the terms of SS which lie in HH. We call SS a regular sequence if

|SH|≤|H|−1for every proper subgroup ​H<G.|S_{H}|\leq|H|-1\qquad\text{for every proper subgroup }H<G.

Let

c0​(G)=min⁡{t:every regular sequence S over G with |S|≥t satisfies Σ⁡(S)=G}.c_{0}(G)=\min\{t:\text{every regular sequence $S$ over $G$ with $|S|\geq t$ satisfies $\Sigma(S)=G$}\}.

Regularity is the natural replacement for the condition that a set is not concentrated in a proper subgroup. It is also useful for sequences with repeated terms: if a sequence is not regular, then redundant terms can be removed until one obtains a regular subsequence with the same set Σ0\Sigma_{0}; see Lemma 2.2.

The problem of determining c0​(G)c_{0}(G) was first proposed by Olson. He conjectured that c0​(Cp⊕Cp)=2​p−1c_{0}(C_{p}\oplus C_{p})=2p-1, which was proved and further studied by Peng [15, 16] in 1987.

Let pp be the smallest prime divisor of |G||G|. Define

(1.1) m⁡(G)={|G|,G​ is cyclic,2​p−1,G≅Cp⊕Cp,p​n+2​p−3,G≅Cp⊕Cp​n​ with ​n≥2,|G|/p+p−2,otherwise.m(G)=\begin{cases}|G|,&G\text{ is cyclic},\\ 2p-1,&G\cong C_{p}\oplus C_{p},\\ pn+2p-3,&G\cong C_{p}\oplus C_{pn}\text{ with }n\geq 2,\\ |G|/p+p-2,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The standard examples give c0​(G)≥m⁡(G)c_{0}(G)\geq m(G); see Lemma 2.3. The following conjecture originates in [4], with the boundary value proposed in [20]; see also [7, 5].

Conjecture 1.1.

For every nontrivial finite abelian group GG,

c0​(G)=m​(G).c_{0}(G)=m(G).

The third case of (1.1) is exceptional. In the other noncyclic cases the usual construction is obtained from a subgroup of index pp and has length |G|/p+p−3|G|/p+p-3. For G=Cp⊕Cp​nG=C_{p}\oplus C_{pn} with n≥2n\geq 2 there is a regular sequence of length p​n+2​p−4pn+2p-4, which is not an additive basis. The equality |G|/p=exp⁡(G)=p​n|G|/p=\exp(G)=pn explains why this family requires a separate argument.

We first record the known results which will be used below. This also gives a precise account of the status of Conjecture 1.1 before presenting our works.

Peng proved

(1.2) c0(Cp⊕Cp)=2p−1,c0(Cpr)=pr−1+p−2(r≥3)c_{0}(C_{p}\oplus C_{p})=2p-1,\qquad c_{0}(C_{p}^{r})=p^{r-1}+p-2\quad(r\geq 3)

for every prime pp [15, 16]. Gao and Hamidoune, and later Gao, et al., determined the cyclic groups, the groups of even order, all groups of rank at least five, and all pp-groups except at that time for the boundary groups Cp⊕CpaC_{p}\oplus C_{p^{a}} [3, 4]. Qu and Han also established an inverse theorem for additive bases [19], and subsequently proved

(1.3) c0​(Cp⊕Cpa)=pa+2​p−3(a≥2)c_{0}(C_{p}\oplus C_{p^{a}})=p^{a}+2p-3\quad(a\geq 2)

[20]. Thus Conjecture 1.1 is known for every finite abelian pp-group. For related inverse results on regular sequences over Cp⊕CpC_{p}\oplus C_{p}, see Peng, Qu, and Li [17].

For groups of higher rank, Gao, Qu, and Zhang proved the following additional cases [7]:

  1. (i)

    rank⁡(G)=4\rank(G)=4, apart from the groups C33⊕CnC_{3}^{3}\oplus C_{n} with 3|n3\mid n, nn odd, not a power of 33, and |G|<3.72×107|G|<3.72\times 10^{7};

  2. (ii)

    rank⁡(G)=3\rank(G)=3 and either the smallest prime divisor pp satisfies p≥11p\geq 11, or 3≤p≤73\leq p\leq 7 and |G|≥3.72×107|G|\geq 3.72\times 10^{7}.

The principal known rank-two results are as follows. Let G=Cn1⊕Cn2G=C_{n_{1}}\oplus C_{n_{2}} with 1<n1|n21<n_{1}\mid n_{2}, and let pp be the smallest prime divisor of |G||G|.

  1. (i)

    If n1≥2​pn_{1}\geq 2p and |G|≥72​p6|G|\geq 72p^{6}, then

    c0​(G)=|G|/p+p−2c_{0}(G)=|G|/p+p-2

    by Gao, Li, Qu, and Wang [5].

  2. (ii)

    If p≥11p\geq 11 and n1≥p2n_{1}\geq p^{2}, then the same equality holds; Qu, Li, Wang, and Zhao also describe the regular nonbases of length c0​(G)−1c_{0}(G)-1 [22].

  3. (iii)

    For every prime q≥5q\geq 5,

    c0​(C3⊕C3​q)=3​q+3c_{0}(C_{3}\oplus C_{3q})=3q+3

    by Qu and Li [21].

Very recently, Yang obtained general upper bounds for c0​(Cq⊕Cn​q)c_{0}(C_{q}\oplus C_{nq}) when the group has odd order, together with related results for a zero-sum invariant [23]. In particular, if qq is prime, n≥2n\geq 2, and p≥3p\geq 3 is the smallest prime divisor of n​qnq, then [23, Theorem 3.5] gives

c0​(Cq⊕Cn​q)≤max⁡{n​q+2​q2−q−1,n​q​(q+1)p−q+p−2}.c_{0}(C_{q}\oplus C_{nq})\leq\max\left\{nq+2q^{2}-q-1,\ \frac{nq(q+1)}{p}-q+p-2\right\}.

For convenience of the reader, the exact values already available in the literature are summarized in Table 1.

Our first result removes all remaining groups of rank at least three.

Theorem 1.2.

If rank⁡(G)≥3\rank(G)\geq 3, then

c0​(G)=m​(G).c_{0}(G)=m(G).

We next settle two basic rank-two families.

Theorem 1.3.

Let p<qp<q be distinct odd primes. Then

c0​(Cp⊕Cp​q)=p​q+2​p−3.c_{0}(C_{p}\oplus C_{pq})=pq+2p-3.
Theorem 1.4.

Let p<qp<q be distinct odd primes. Then

c0​(Cq⊕Cp​q)=q2+p−2.c_{0}(C_{q}\oplus C_{pq})=q^{2}+p-2.

The next theorem deals with groups with first invariant factor divisible by p2p^{2} and having no other prime divisor.

Theorem 1.5.

Let pp be an odd prime, let 2≤a≤b2\leq a\leq b, and let nn be a positive integer with no prime divisor smaller than pp. Then

c0​(Cpa⊕Cpb​n)=pa+b−1​n+p−2.c_{0}(C_{p^{a}}\oplus C_{p^{b}n})=p^{a+b-1}n+p-2.

Combining these results gives a complete answer outside the boundary family.

Corollary 1.6.

Let GG be a nontrivial finite abelian group and let pp be the smallest prime divisor of |G||G|. If GG is not isomorphic to Cp⊕Cp​nC_{p}\oplus C_{pn} for any integer n≥2n\geq 2, then

c0​(G)=m​(G).c_{0}(G)=m(G).

For the boundary family we obtain a complete result when the smallest prime is 33.

Theorem 1.7.

For every odd integer n≥3n\geq 3,

c0​(C3⊕C3​n)=3​n+3.c_{0}(C_{3}\oplus C_{3n})=3n+3.
Corollary 1.8.

If the smallest prime divisor of |G||G| is 33, then

c0​(G)=m​(G).c_{0}(G)=m(G).

In Section 2 we present some preliminaries and auxiliary results. We provide a reduction argument in Section 3, and the theorem for groups of rank at least three is proved in Section 4. Section 5 gives the estimates for cosets of a cyclic subgroup and proves Theorems 1.3 and 1.4. The lifting argument in Section 6 proves Theorem 1.5 and Corollary 1.6. The groups Cp⊕Cp​nC_{p}\oplus C_{pn} are considered in Section 7, and the proof for p=3p=3 is given in Section 8.

2. Preliminaries

We use the notation introduced in Section 1. For g∈Gg\in G and k≥0k\geq 0, let g[k]g^{[k]} denote the sequence consisting of kk copies of gg. If T|ST\mid S, then S​T−1ST^{-1} is obtained by deleting the terms of TT, with their multiplicities. The support of SS is denoted by supp⁡(S)\operatorname{supp}(S), and ⟨A⟩\langle A\rangle denotes the subgroup generated by A⊆GA\subseteq G. For a nonempty subset AA of GG, put

st⁡(A)={g∈G:g+A=A}.\operatorname{st}(A)=\{g\in G:g+A=A\}.

We say that AA has trivial stabilizer if st⁡(A)={0}\operatorname{st}(A)=\{0\}. We use

Σ0​(S​T)=Σ0​(S)+Σ0​(T),st⁡(Σ0​(S))⊆st⁡(Σ0​(S​T)).\Sigma_{0}(ST)=\Sigma_{0}(S)+\Sigma_{0}(T),\qquad\operatorname{st}(\Sigma_{0}(S))\subseteq\operatorname{st}(\Sigma_{0}(ST)).

We first recall Kneser’s theorem [13]; see also [8, 9, 14] for detailed discussion.

Theorem 2.1 (Kneser).

Let A1,…,AtA_{1},\ldots,A_{t} be finite nonempty subsets of an abelian group, and let H=st⁡(A1+⋯+At)H=\operatorname{st}(A_{1}+\cdots+A_{t}). Then

|A1+⋯+At|≥∑i=1t|Ai+H|−(t−1)​|H|.|A_{1}+\cdots+A_{t}|\geq\sum_{i=1}^{t}|A_{i}+H|-(t-1)|H|.

In particular, if H={0}H=\{0\}, then

|A1+⋯+At|≥1+∑i=1t(|Ai|−1).|A_{1}+\cdots+A_{t}|\geq 1+\sum_{i=1}^{t}(|A_{i}|-1).

The Davenport constant 𝖣⁡(G)\mathsf{D}(G) is the least positive integer dd such that every sequence over GG of length at least dd has a nonempty zero-sum subsequence; see [12] for a recent study and references therein. We shall use

(2.1) 𝖣(G)≤m(G),𝖣(Cm⊕Cn)=m+n−1(1≤m∣n);\mathsf{D}(G)\leq m(G),\qquad\mathsf{D}(C_{m}\oplus C_{n})=m+n-1\quad(1\leq m\mid n);

see [4, Lemmas 2.6 and 2.7] and [7, Lemma 2.5]. We also use 𝖣⁡(G)≤|G|\mathsf{D}(G)\leq|G|. For the trivial group we take c0​({0})=𝖣⁡({0})=1c_{0}(\{0\})=\mathsf{D}(\{0\})=1.

The following three results are already known.

Lemma 2.2 ([7, Lemma 2.2]).

If a sequence SS over GG is not regular, then it has a proper regular subsequence TT such that Σ0​(T)=Σ0​(S)\Sigma_{0}(T)=\Sigma_{0}(S).

Lemma 2.3 ([7, Lemma 2.3]).

For every nontrivial finite abelian group GG, we have c0​(G)≥m⁡(G)c_{0}(G)\geq m(G).

Lemma 2.4 ([4, Lemma 2.3]).

Let pp be the smallest prime divisor of |G||G|, and let SS be a regular sequence with

|S|≥max⁡{|G|/p+p−2,𝖣⁡(G)}.|S|\geq\max\{|G|/p+p-2,\mathsf{D}(G)\}.

If Σ⁡(S)≠G\Sigma(S)\neq G, then 0∈Σ⁡(S)0\in\Sigma(S) and, for every nonempty subsequence T|ST\mid S,

st⁡(Σ0​(T))={0},|Σ0​(T)|≥|T|+1.\operatorname{st}(\Sigma_{0}(T))=\{0\},\qquad|\Sigma_{0}(T)|\geq|T|+1.

To keep the later estimates short, we denote

(2.2) e⁡(T)=|Σ0​(T)|−|T|−1.e(T)=|\Sigma_{0}(T)|-|T|-1.

Thus e⁡(1)=0e(1)=0, and Lemma 2.4 gives e⁡(T)≥0e(T)\geq 0 for every T|ST\mid S under its hypotheses.

Lemma 2.5.

Let TT be a sequence over GG and g∈G∖{0}g\in G\setminus\{0\}. If Σ0​(T)\Sigma_{0}(T) has trivial stabilizer, then e⁡(T​g)≥e⁡(T)e(Tg)\geq e(T).

Proof.

Since g∉st⁡(Σ0​(T))g\notin\operatorname{st}(\Sigma_{0}(T)), the set Σ0​(T)∪(g+Σ0​(T))\Sigma_{0}(T)\cup(g+\Sigma_{0}(T)) has at least one more element than Σ0​(T)\Sigma_{0}(T). ∎

We shall also use the following consequence of the Cauchy–Davenport theorem [1].

Lemma 2.6.

Let pp be prime and let UU be a sequence of nonzero elements of CpC_{p}. Then

|Σ0​(U)|≥min⁡{p,|U|+1}.|\Sigma_{0}(U)|\geq\min\{p,|U|+1\}.

In particular, Σ0​(U)=Cp\Sigma_{0}(U)=C_{p} if |U|≥p−1|U|\geq p-1.

Lemma 2.7.

Let H≤GH\leq G, let AA be a sequence over HH, and let TT be a sequence over GG. If φ:G⟶G/H\varphi:G\longrightarrow G/H is the natural homomorphism, then

|Σ0​(A​T)|≥|Σ0​(A)|​|Σ0​(φ⁡(T))|.|\Sigma_{0}(AT)|\geq|\Sigma_{0}(A)|\,|\Sigma_{0}(\varphi(T))|.
Proof.

For each γ∈Σ0​(φ⁡(T))\gamma\in\Sigma_{0}(\varphi(T)), choose Tγ|TT_{\gamma}\mid T with φ⁡(σ⁡(Tγ))=γ\varphi(\sigma(T_{\gamma}))=\gamma. The sets σ⁡(Tγ)+Σ0​(A)\sigma(T_{\gamma})+\Sigma_{0}(A) lie in distinct cosets of HH and are contained in Σ0​(A​T)\Sigma_{0}(AT). ∎

Lemma 2.8 ([4, Lemma 2.4]).

For every finite abelian group AA, we have c0​(A)≤|A|c_{0}(A)\leq|A|.

Lemma 2.9.

Let WW be a sequence of nonzero elements of a finite abelian group AA. If Σ0​(W)\Sigma_{0}(W) has trivial stabilizer, then WW is regular over AA.

Proof.

Otherwise choose a proper subgroup J<AJ<A of least order with |WJ|≥|J||W_{J}|\geq|J|. Then J≠{0}J\neq\{0\} and WJW_{J} is regular over JJ. Lemma 2.8 gives Σ0​(WJ)=J\Sigma_{0}(W_{J})=J, so Σ0​(W)=J+Σ0​(W​WJ−1)\Sigma_{0}(W)=J+\Sigma_{0}(WW_{J}^{-1}) is stabilized by JJ, a contradiction. ∎

The next lemma allows us to retain a prescribed regular subsequence when choosing a short subsequence with all possible subset sums.

Lemma 2.10.

Let XX be a sequence over a finite abelian group AA with Σ0​(X)=A\Sigma_{0}(X)=A. Suppose that Z|XZ\mid X is regular over AA and |Z|≤c0​(A)−1|Z|\leq c_{0}(A)-1. Then there is a subsequence R|XR\mid X such that

Z|R,|R|≤c0​(A),Σ0​(R)=A.Z\mid R,\qquad|R|\leq c_{0}(A),\qquad\Sigma_{0}(R)=A.
Proof.

We delete terms outside ZZ, preserving the set of subset sums, until the remaining sequence is regular. To make this more precise, let YY be the current sequence. If it is not regular, choose J<AJ<A with |YJ|≥|J||Y_{J}|\geq|J|, and write

YJ=ZJy1⋯ym,t=|ZJ|≤|J|−1.Y_{J}=Z_{J}y_{1}\cdots y_{m},\qquad t=|Z_{J}|\leq|J|-1.

We first show that |Σ0​(ZJ)|≥t+1|\Sigma_{0}(Z_{J})|\geq t+1. Put H=st⁡(Σ0​(ZJ))H=\operatorname{st}(\Sigma_{0}(Z_{J})) and h=|H|h=|H|. Since H⊆Σ0​(ZJ)H\subseteq\Sigma_{0}(Z_{J}), the assertion is immediate if h≥t+1h\geq t+1. Otherwise H<JH<J, and regularity gives |ZH|≤h−1|Z_{H}|\leq h-1. Theorem 2.1 therefore yields

|Σ0​(ZJ)|≥(t+2−h)​h≥t+1,|\Sigma_{0}(Z_{J})|\geq(t+2-h)h\geq t+1,

where the last inequality is equivalent to (h−1)​(t−h+1)≥0(h-1)(t-h+1)\geq 0.

Starting from Σ0​(ZJ)\Sigma_{0}(Z_{J}), adjoin y1,…,ymy_{1},\ldots,y_{m} successively. If every term enlarged the sumset, the final set would have at least t+1+m=|YJ|+1>|J|t+1+m=|Y_{J}|+1>|J| elements. Hence one of these terms can be deleted without changing Σ0​(YJ)\Sigma_{0}(Y_{J}), and therefore without changing Σ0​(Y)\Sigma_{0}(Y).

The process ends with a regular subsequence Y′|XY^{\prime}\mid X containing ZZ and satisfying Σ0​(Y′)=A\Sigma_{0}(Y^{\prime})=A. If |Y′|≤c0​(A)|Y^{\prime}|\leq c_{0}(A), take R=Y′R=Y^{\prime}. Otherwise take any c0​(A)c_{0}(A) terms of Y′Y^{\prime} that include ZZ; their sequence is regular and is an additive basis of AA. ∎

We need the following two facts concerning Cp2C_{p}^{2}. The equality for c0​(Cp2)c_{0}(C_{p}^{2}) is due to Peng [15, Theorem 2]; the additional estimate follows from [6, Theorem 3.12] (see also [21, Lemma 2.4]).

Theorem 2.11.

Let pp be prime. Then c0​(Cp2)=2​p−1c_{0}(C_{p}^{2})=2p-1. Moreover, if YY is regular over Cp2C_{p}^{2} and |Y|=2​p−2|Y|=2p-2, then |Σ0​(Y)|≥p2−1|\Sigma_{0}(Y)|\geq p^{2}-1.

Lemma 2.12.

If YY is a sequence over Cp2C_{p}^{2} with Σ0​(Y)=Cp2\Sigma_{0}(Y)=C_{p}^{2}, then it has a subsequence CC with Σ0​(C)=Cp2\Sigma_{0}(C)=C_{p}^{2} such that either |C|≤2​p−2|C|\leq 2p-2, or |C|=2​p−1|C|=2p-1 and CC is regular.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.2, we may replace YY by a regular subsequence with the same subset sums. If its length exceeds 2​p−22p-2, take any 2​p−12p-1 of its terms and apply Theorem 2.11. ∎

3. A reduction argument

Let qq be prime and let π:G⟶Cq2\pi:G\longrightarrow C_{q}^{2} be surjective. For every subgroup M≤Cq2M\leq C_{q}^{2} of order qq, let HM=π−1​(M)H_{M}=\pi^{-1}(M). We first recall a consequence of Hall’s marriage theorem [10]. In the form needed here, that theorem states that a finite family of sets E1,…,EtE_{1},\ldots,E_{t} has distinct representatives xi∈Eix_{i}\in E_{i} if and only if

|⋃i∈IEi|≥|I|for every ​I⊆{1,…,t}.\left|\bigcup_{i\in I}E_{i}\right|\geq|I|\quad\text{for every }I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,t\}.

When this theorem is applied to a sequence, different occurrences of the same group element are regarded as distinct choices.

Lemma 3.1.

Let ℒ\mathcal{L} be a collection of subgroups of Cq2C_{q}^{2} of order qq, and let ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1. Suppose that, for every nonempty 𝒥⊆ℒ\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{L}, at least ℓ​|𝒥|\ell|\mathcal{J}| terms of a sequence SS lie outside at least one of the subgroups HMH_{M}, M∈𝒥M\in\mathcal{J}. Then there are pairwise disjoint subsequences TM|ST_{M}\mid S, M∈ℒM\in\mathcal{L}, such that |TM|=ℓ|T_{M}|=\ell and all terms of TMT_{M} lie outside HMH_{M}.

Proof.

For each M∈ℒM\in\mathcal{L}, take ℓ\ell copies of the set of occurrences in SS outside HMH_{M}. A collection of copies involving precisely the members of 𝒥\mathcal{J} has at most ℓ​|𝒥|\ell|\mathcal{J}| members, while their union has at least this many occurrences by hypothesis. Hall’s theorem gives the required choices. ∎

Now we present the setting we use throughout this section. Suppose that p<qp<q are odd primes, that pp is the smallest prime divisor of |G||G|, and that GG has a quotient Cq2C_{q}^{2}. Write

π:G⟶Cq2,K=ker⁡π,|G|=p​q2​h,|K|=p​h.\pi:G\longrightarrow C_{q}^{2},\qquad K=\ker\pi,\qquad|G|=pq^{2}h,\qquad|K|=ph.

Assume that m⁡(G)=|G|/p+p−2m(G)=|G|/p+p-2, and put

L=q2​h+p−2,N=|G|−1−L=(p−1)​q2​h−p+1.L=q^{2}h+p-2,\qquad N=|G|-1-L=(p-1)q^{2}h-p+1.
Theorem 3.2.

In the preceding setting, suppose that integers r,ℓr,\ell satisfy 1≤r≤q+11\leq r\leq q+1, 1≤ℓ≤q−11\leq\ell\leq q-1, and

(3.1) r​ℓ​Lq+1\displaystyle\frac{r\ell L}{q+1} ≥N,\displaystyle\geq N,
(3.2) ℓ⁡(L−r​ℓ)\displaystyle\ell(L-r\ell) ≥N,\displaystyle\geq N,
(3.3) h⁡(q2−p)+p−1\displaystyle h(q^{2}-p)+p-1 ≥r​ℓ.\displaystyle\geq r\ell.

Then c0​(G)=Lc_{0}(G)=L.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.3, it suffices to prove the upper bound. Suppose that SS is regular, |S|=L|S|=L, and Σ⁡(S)≠G\Sigma(S)\neq G. By (2.1) and Lemma 2.4, every Σ0​(T)\Sigma_{0}(T), T|ST\mid S, has trivial stabilizer.

Lemma 5.1.

Lemma 8.1.

Let AA be a sequence of nonzero elements of an abelian group of odd order, and suppose that st⁡(Σ0​(A))={0}\operatorname{st}(\Sigma_{0}(A))=\{0\}.

  1. (i)

    If e⁡(A)≥2e(A)\geq 2, then some B|AB\mid A satisfies |B|≤3|B|\leq 3 and e⁡(B)≥2e(B)\geq 2.

  2. (ii)

    If e⁡(A)=0e(A)=0, then Σ0​(A)\Sigma_{0}(A) is an arithmetic progression of size |A|+1|A|+1.

  3. (iii)

    If e⁡(A)=1e(A)=1 and |A|≥3|A|\geq 3, then Σ0​(A)\Sigma_{0}(A) is an arithmetic progression of size |A|+2|A|+2.

Proof.

Every subsequence of AA also has a subset-sum set with trivial stabilizer. Thus e⁡(B)≤e⁡(A)e(B)\leq e(A) for B|AB\mid A, by Lemma 2.5. The assertions for |A|≤2|A|\leq 2 are immediate.

Suppose that |A|≥3|A|\geq 3 and that e⁡(B)≤1e(B)\leq 1 whenever B|AB\mid A and |B|≤3|B|\leq 3. If every two-term subsequence has value zero, then any two terms x,yx,y satisfy

|{0,x,y,x+y}|=3.|\{0,x,y,x+y\}|=3.

Hence y=xy=x or y=−xy=-x, and all terms of AA belong to {g,−g}\{g,-g\} for some nonzero gg. Their subset sums form an interval in ⟨g⟩\langle g\rangle. This interval cannot fill ⟨g⟩\langle g\rangle, since its stabilizer is trivial, and therefore it has exactly |A|+1|A|+1 elements.

Otherwise choose two terms x,yx,y for which

Q={0,x,y,x+y}Q=\{0,x,y,x+y\}

has four elements. For every other term zz, our assumption gives

|Q∪(Q+z)|=5,|Q∩(Q+z)|=3.|Q\cup(Q+z)|=5,\qquad|Q\cap(Q+z)|=3.

The three edges u⟶u+zu\longrightarrow u+z within QQ form either one path of length three, or a cycle of length three and an isolated point. The latter possibility would put three points of QQ in one coset of a subgroup of order three and the fourth point in a different coset. This is incompatible with the equality of the sums of the opposite pairs of QQ. Consequently

Q=a+{0,d,2​d,3​d}Q=a+\{0,d,2d,3d\}

for some dd of odd order N≥5N\geq 5. Since 0∈Q0\in Q, this progression lies in ⟨d⟩\langle d\rangle. The case N=5N=5 would give Σ0​(x​y​z)=⟨d⟩\Sigma_{0}(xyz)=\langle d\rangle, so N≥7N\geq 7.

It is not hard to verify that a four-term progression in a cyclic group of odd order at least seven has three points in common with a nonzero translate only when the translation is dd or −d-d. Thus every term other than x,yx,y belongs to {d,−d}\{d,-d\}. The only pairing of the positions 0,1,2,30,1,2,3 with equal pair sums modulo NN is {0,3},{1,2}\{0,3\},\{1,2\}. It follows that one of x,yx,y belongs to {d,−d}\{d,-d\} and the other to {2​d,−2​d}\{2d,-2d\}. Therefore all but one terms of AA belong to {d,−d}\{d,-d\}, and the remaining term is 2​d2d or −2​d-2d. The subset sums of the former terms form an interval of at least three points. Adding the remaining term gives another interval, of at most |A|+2|A|+2 points. In particular, e⁡(A)≤1e(A)\leq 1, proving (i) by contraposition.

If e⁡(A)=0e(A)=0, monotonicity implies that every pair has value zero, so the case where every pair has value zero proves (ii). If e⁡(A)=1e(A)=1 and |A|≥3|A|\geq 3, some pair has value one; otherwise the first part of the argument would give e⁡(A)=0e(A)=0. The preceding argument then shows that Σ0​(A)\Sigma_{0}(A) is a progression. Its size is |A|+2|A|+2 by definition, proving (iii). ∎

Lemma 8.2.

Let φ:G⟶C3\varphi:G\longrightarrow C_{3} be surjective, and let TT be a sequence of five terms with nonzero images. If st⁡(Σ0​(T))={0}\operatorname{st}(\Sigma_{0}(T))=\{0\}, then each coset of ker⁡φ\ker\varphi contains at least two elements of Σ0​(T)\Sigma_{0}(T).

Proof.

Write the two nonzero images as 11 and −1-1, choosing the sign so that at least three terms have image 11. Let b∈{0,1,2}b\in\{0,1,2\} be the number with image −1-1. Every quotient element is represented by a subset sum, by Lemma 2.6. We show that none has only one representative.

Suppose first that the only subset sum with image zero is 00. If both signs occur, every term with image −1-1 is the negative of every term with image 11. Thus all positive-image terms equal some gg, and three such terms give 3​g=03g=0. If all five images are 11, comparison of overlapping triples gives the same conclusion.

Suppose next that there is only one subset sum with image 11. All terms with that image equal some gg. If b=0b=0, comparing a one-term sum with a four-term sum gives g=4​gg=4g. If b=1b=1, write hh for the remaining term. Comparing gg with 2​g+h2g+h gives h=−gh=-g, and again 4​g=g4g=g. If b=2b=2, the same comparison gives h1=h2=−gh_{1}=h_{2}=-g; their sum then gives −2​g=g-2g=g.

Finally, suppose that there is only one subset sum with image −1-1. Comparison of the sums of two positive-image terms shows that all positive-image terms equal some gg. Every negative-image term equals 2​g2g. If b=0b=0, compare 2​g2g with 5​g5g. If b=1b=1, compare hh with 3​g+h3g+h. If b=2b=2, compare h1h_{1} with g+h1+h2g+h_{1}+h_{2}.

In every case, all terms belong to {g,−g}\{g,-g\} with 3​g=03g=0. Since φ⁡(g)≠0\varphi(g)\neq 0, this gives Σ0​(T)=⟨g⟩\Sigma_{0}(T)=\langle g\rangle with nontrivial stabilizer, a contradiction. ∎

Lemma 8.3.

For the four subsequences PiP_{i} defined above,

∑i=03e⁡(Pi)≤1.\sum_{i=0}^{3}e(P_{i})\leq 1.
Proof.

Suppose that e⁡(Pi)≥2e(P_{i})\geq 2 for some ii. By Lemma 8.1, there is a subsequence B|PiB\mid P_{i} of length three with e⁡(B)≥2e(B)\geq 2. If eight terms satisfying (8.1) can be chosen outside BB, then BB remains in Pi​Ri−1P_{i}R_{i}^{-1}, contradicting (8.2).

Otherwise, let aja_{j} be the number of terms remaining in PjP_{j} after BB is removed. Then

∑jaj=3​n,∑jmin⁡{6,aj}≤7.\sum_{j}a_{j}=3n,\qquad\sum_{j}\min\{6,a_{j}\}\leq 7.

so Σ0​(Pj)=Hj\Sigma_{0}(P_{j})=H_{j}, contrary to Lemma 2.4. Thus e⁡(Pi)≤1e(P_{i})\leq 1 for every ii.

If eight terms satisfying (8.1) can be removed from the rest, the two pairs contradict (8.2). Since Σ0​(Pj)⊆Hj\Sigma_{0}(P_{j})\subseteq H_{j} has trivial stabilizer, we must have

|Pj|=3​n−2,e⁡(Pj)=0,Σ0​(Pj)=Hj∖{h}|P_{j}|=3n-2,\qquad e(P_{j})=0,\qquad\Sigma_{0}(P_{j})=H_{j}\setminus\{h\}

for some h∈Hjh\in H_{j}. The remaining five terms of SS lie outside HjH_{j}. By Lemma 8.2, their subset sums have two distinct elements in each HjH_{j}-coset. The corresponding two translates of Hj∖{h}H_{j}\setminus\{h\} fill that coset. Hence Σ0​(S)=G\Sigma_{0}(S)=G, again a contradiction. ∎

Lemma 8.4.

Let NN be odd, let 2≤k≤42\leq k\leq 4, and let A1,…,AkA_{1},\ldots,A_{k} be nonempty arithmetic progressions in CNC_{N}. Suppose that the differences of those progressions having at least two elements generate CNC_{N}. If

∑i=1k|Ai|≥N+k−1,\sum_{i=1}^{k}|A_{i}|\geq N+k-1,

then A1+⋯+Ak=CNA_{1}+\cdots+A_{k}=C_{N}.

Proof.

Suppose that the sum is proper, and let H=st⁡(A1+⋯+Ak)H=\operatorname{st}(A_{1}+\cdots+A_{k}). If H={0}H=\{0\}, Theorem 2.1 immediately gives a contradiction. Otherwise, writing

h=|H|,t=[CN:H],h=|H|,\qquad t=[C_{N}:H],

we have h,t≥3h,t\geq 3.

Let rr be the number of progressions having at least two elements whose differences do not belong to HH. The sum of the images in CN/HC_{N}/H has trivial stabilizer. For each of these rr progressions, its size is smaller than the order of its difference in the quotient. Indeed, otherwise its image would be a coset of a nontrivial subgroup, which would stabilize the quotient sumset. Its image therefore has the same size as the progression itself. Each of the remaining s=k−rs=k-r progressions has a singleton image and contains at most hh elements.

Theorem 2.1 shows that

∑i​ among ther​ progressions|Ai|≤t+r−2.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\text{ among the}\\ r\text{ progressions}\end{subarray}}|A_{i}|\leq t+r-2.

The generating assumption gives r≥1r\geq 1, so s≤k−1≤3≤ts\leq k-1\leq 3\leq t. Consequently

∑i=1k|Ai|≤t+r−2+s​h<N+k−1,\sum_{i=1}^{k}|A_{i}|\leq t+r-2+sh<N+k-1,

because the difference between the last two bounds is

N+k−1−(t+r−2+s​h)=(h−1)​(t−s)+1>0.N+k-1-(t+r-2+sh)=(h-1)(t-s)+1>0.

This is the required contradiction. ∎

By Lemmas 8.1 and 8.3, every Σ0​(Pi)\Sigma_{0}(P_{i}) is an arithmetic progression, except possibly when |Pi|=2|P_{i}|=2 and e⁡(Pi)=1e(P_{i})=1. When all four sumsets are progressions, write

(8.3) Σ0​(Pi)=ai+{0,gi,…,ℓi​gi},ℓi=|Pi|+e⁡(Pi).\Sigma_{0}(P_{i})=a_{i}+\{0,g_{i},\ldots,\ell_{i}g_{i}\},\qquad\ell_{i}=|P_{i}|+e(P_{i}).

For an empty PiP_{i}, take ai=0a_{i}=0, ℓi=0\ell_{i}=0, and choose any gig_{i} whose image is nonzero in the assigned subgroup of VV. For a nonempty PiP_{i}, consecutive points of the progression show that gi∈Hig_{i}\in H_{i}. Since the progression contains zero and a term outside KK, its difference is not in KK. Thus gi+Kg_{i}+K is nonzero in the assigned subgroup in every case. Moreover, the trivial stabilizer gives

ord⁡(gi)=3​ord⁡(di).\operatorname{ord}(g_{i})=3\operatorname{ord}(d_{i}).

Proof.

∑i=03ℓi≤max⁡{16,12​n/5−8}<3​n+3,\sum_{i=0}^{3}\ell_{i}\leq\max\{16,12n/5-8\}<3n+3,

G=⟨e⟩⊕⟨f⟩,ord⁡(e)=3,ord⁡(f)=3​n.G=\langle e\rangle\oplus\langle f\rangle,\qquad\operatorname{ord}(e)=3,\quad\operatorname{ord}(f)=3n.

Proof of Theorem 1.7.

The lower bound follows from Lemma 2.3. The case n=3n=3 follows from the known result for finite abelian 33-groups [20]. Let n≥5n\geq 5 be odd, and suppose that a regular sequence SS of length 3​n+33n+3 is not an additive basis. The preceding results apply.

First suppose that all four sumsets have the form (8.3), and put

ε=∑i=03e⁡(Pi)∈{0,1},∑i=03ℓi=3​n+3+ε.\varepsilon=\sum_{i=0}^{3}e(P_{i})\in\{0,1\},\qquad\sum_{i=0}^{3}\ell_{i}=3n+3+\varepsilon.

Every ℓi\ell_{i} is at most 3​n−23n-2, by (8.4), so at least two of them are at least two.

Fix a target element of VV, and subtract the image of ∑iai\sum_{i}a_{i} to obtain x∈Vx\in V. Write vi=gi+Kv_{i}=g_{i}+K. For r∈{0,1,2}r\in\{0,1,2\}, let si​(r)s_{i}(r) be the number of integers in [0,ℓi][0,\ell_{i}] congruent to rr modulo three. The corresponding part of the progression, when nonempty, is a translate of a progression in KK with difference did_{i} and size si​(r)s_{i}(r), and

si​(0)+si​(1)+si​(2)=ℓi+1.s_{i}(0)+s_{i}(1)+s_{i}(2)=\ell_{i}+1.

If ℓi≥2\ell_{i}\geq 2, all three parts are nonempty. If ℓi≤1\ell_{i}\leq 1, every nonempty part is a singleton. If ℓi≥5\ell_{i}\geq 5, every part has at least two elements. Thus, whenever parts from all indices with ℓi≥5\ell_{i}\geq 5 are selected, their nonsingleton differences generate KK by Lemma 8.5.

Suppose first that all four ℓi\ell_{i} are at least two. The equation

r0​v0+r1​v1+r2​v2+r3​v3=x,ri∈{0,1,2},r_{0}v_{0}+r_{1}v_{1}+r_{2}v_{2}+r_{3}v_{3}=x,\qquad r_{i}\in\{0,1,2\},

has nine solutions. Each coefficient takes each value exactly three times, since any two distinct viv_{i} generate VV. The average of ∑isi​(ri)\sum_{i}s_{i}(r_{i}) over these solutions is

13​∑i=03(ℓi+1)=3​n+7+ε3>n+2.\frac{1}{3}\sum_{i=0}^{3}(\ell_{i}+1)=\frac{3n+7+\varepsilon}{3}>n+2.

Some solution therefore selects four nonempty progressions whose total size is at least n+3n+3. Lemma 8.4 shows that their sum fills the chosen coset of KK.

Suppose next that exactly three ℓi\ell_{i} are at least two. Fix a nonempty part of the remaining progression, whose parameter is t≤1t\leq 1. The coefficient equation in the other three directions has three solutions, and each coefficient takes each value once. The average total size of these three selected parts is

3​n+6+ε−t3>n+1.\frac{3n+6+\varepsilon-t}{3}>n+1.

One solution therefore has total size at least n+2n+2. All indices with ℓi≥5\ell_{i}\geq 5 occur among these three, so Lemma 8.4 again fills the chosen coset.

It remains to consider exactly two indices with ℓi≥2\ell_{i}\geq 2, say i=0,1i=0,1. Put

mi=ℓi+1,qi=⌊mi3⌋(i=0,1),t=ℓ2+ℓ3≤2.m_{i}=\ell_{i}+1,\qquad q_{i}=\left\lfloor\frac{m_{i}}{3}\right\rfloor\quad(i=0,1),\qquad t=\ell_{2}+\ell_{3}\leq 2.

Then

m0+m1=3​n+5+ε−t≥3​n+3,q0+q1≥n.m_{0}+m_{1}=3n+5+\varepsilon-t\geq 3n+3,\qquad q_{0}+q_{1}\geq n.

After nonempty parts of the two small progressions are fixed, the two coefficients r0,r1r_{0},r_{1} are uniquely determined. If q0+q1≥n+1q_{0}+q_{1}\geq n+1, the selected parts already have total size at least n+1n+1.

Suppose that q0+q1=nq_{0}+q_{1}=n. The remainders mi−3​qim_{i}-3q_{i} have sum at least three, so one of them is two. Also t≥1t\geq 1, since otherwise their sum would be at least five, whereas each remainder is at most two. In the progression with remainder two, two parts have size qi+1q_{i}+1 and only one has size qiq_{i}. Choose j∈{2,3}j\in\{2,3\} with ℓj=1\ell_{j}=1, and vary its coefficient between zero and one while keeping the other small coefficient fixed. Both r0r_{0} and r1r_{1} change, since vjv_{j} belongs to neither of their subgroups. At least one choice therefore selects a part of size qi+1q_{i}+1 in the progression with remainder two. The two large parts then have total size at least n+1n+1.

In both alternatives the two selected parts are nonempty, and their nonsingleton differences include all did_{i} with ℓi≥5\ell_{i}\geq 5. Lemma 8.4 fills the chosen coset. Since the target was arbitrary, this proves Σ0​(S)=G\Sigma_{0}(S)=G when all four sumsets are progressions.

Finally, suppose that one PiP_{i} consists of two terms, has e⁡(Pi)=1e(P_{i})=1, and its sumset is not a progression. The other three sequences have value zero and total length 3​n+13n+1. Write their sumsets in the form (8.3); for them ℓi=|Pi|\ell_{i}=|P_{i}|. Their elements did_{i} with ℓi≥5\ell_{i}\geq 5 generate KK. Indeed, if the generated subgroup had index at least five, the argument of Lemma 8.5 would give

∑iℓi≤max⁡{12,9​n/5−6}<3​n+1.\sum_{i}\ell_{i}\leq\max\{12,9n/5-6\}<3n+1.

If its index were three, at most one of the three parameters could be at least five, giving

∑iℓi≤n−2+8=n+6<3​n+1.\sum_{i}\ell_{i}\leq n-2+8=n+6<3n+1.

Both are impossible.

At least two of these three parameters are at least two; otherwise their total would be at most (3​n−2)+2=3​n(3n-2)+2=3n. If all three are at least two, choose the empty subsequence from the exceptional sequence. For each target in VV, the other three coefficients have three solutions and each takes each value once. Their average total size is

(3​n+1)+33=n+43.\frac{(3n+1)+3}{3}=n+\frac{4}{3}.

Some solution has total size at least n+2n+2, so Lemma 8.4 fills the target coset.

If just two progression parameters are at least two, fix a nonempty part of the third, whose parameter is t≤1t\leq 1. The projected subset sums of the exceptional two-term sequence cover its subgroup of order three. Choose one actual subset sum for each of those three images. As the image varies, the uniquely determined coefficients in the two remaining directions each take every value once. The average total size of their parts is

3​n+3−t3>n.\frac{3n+3-t}{3}>n.

Thus one choice gives two nonempty progressions of total size at least n+1n+1. Their nonsingleton differences include all the generating did_{i} with ℓi≥5\ell_{i}\geq 5. Lemma 8.4 again fills the target coset. This proves Σ0​(S)=G\Sigma_{0}(S)=G in the last case, completing the desired contradiction. ∎

Proof of Corollary 1.8.

By Corollary 1.6, it remains to consider G=C3⊕C3​nG=C_{3}\oplus C_{3n}, where nn is odd. For n=1n=1, the result is Theorem 2.11; for n≥3n\geq 3, it follows from Theorem 1.7. ∎
